description: We are Mayara Martins and Lucas C. Xavier (medicine) and Abrahan Duarte (agronomy), from Ciudad del Este, Paraguay. GeoCare Life shows the health risks of the place where you live: heat, floods, drought, dengue, air and river pollution. Using 40+ years of NASA data, it tests which changes are real and turns them into clear prevention for you, your family and your home.
summary:
geocare.life is an Earth System Trend Detective for any address on Earth. You choose a place. The app takes eight climate variables from NASA data, builds a yearly series from 1981 to 2025 for each one, measures the rate of change with the Theil-Sen slope and tests its significance with the Mann-Kendall test. Using yearly values removes the seasonal cycle. A trend is called "confirmed" only when two independent datasets, NASA POWER and ERA5, both show a significant change in the same direction. When the data cannot prove a change, the app says so.
Then it answers twice: with the data, for the specialist, and in plain words, for everyone else. The idea came from a clinic in Ciudad del Este, Paraguay. The physician on our team sees that weather information does not reach people in a form they can use: "They say it will rain, but what does that mean for me?" This week one of the patients fainted in a market on a hot day. So geocare.life asks where you live and, if you want, who you are. It then says what this week means for you, what the next months tend to bring, whether the climate has changed there, whether the ground is safe, and what to do.
details:
Links. App: https://geocare.life/?lang=en · Planet view: https://geocare.life/earth/ · Step-by-step guide: https://geocare.life/tutorial/ · Code: https://github.com/Alex0Luz/geocare

The detective: what the tool does

geocare.life detects trends in Earth system data for one place and says how sure it is. Type an address, tap the map or use your location. The app then does the four things the challenge asks for.

  1. Select variables. Eight signals, each defined in one plain sentence: average temperature, very hot days, yearly rainfall, heavy-rain days, dry days, air humidity, topsoil wetness, and the length of the season that is thermally suitable for dengue transmission.
  2. Choose a region. Any point on Earth. A grid of 5 × 5 NASA POWER points around the address shows where temperature or rainfall is changing. Two addresses can be compared side by side. A world panorama applies the same test to 300 large cities in 106 countries.
  3. See the time series. Each signal shows its direction and its rate per decade. Tapping it opens the evidence: the yearly series from 1981 to 2025 with its trend line, the first and the last ten years shaded with their averages, the total change, and a table with one row per data source. The data can be exported as CSV.
  4. Test the trend. Every series goes through the Mann-Kendall test (significant when p is below 0.05) and the Theil-Sen slope with a 95% confidence interval. The test runs on yearly values, so the seasonal cycle does not count as a trend. Six of the eight signals have two independent sources, NASA POWER (MERRA-2) and ERA5. The app gives one of five verdicts: confirmed (both significant, same direction), likely (one significant, the other pointing the same way), sources disagree, one source only, or no clear trend. Air humidity and topsoil wetness have one source, so they can never be "confirmed".

For 18 places the app adds official series from the NASA Giovanni Time Series Service as extra witnesses in the same table: MERRA-2 daily temperature, AIRS surface air temperature and GPM IMERG rainfall. For those places it also shows nitrogen dioxide (OMI), groundwater (GRACE) and soil moisture (GLDAS).

Why two sources

While building geocare.life we found that one dataset alone can mislead. In our own city, Ciudad del Este, MERRA-2 shows nights of 24 °C or more going from about 25 a year in 1981–1990 to about 48 in 2016–2025. ERA5 shows about 28 in both decades. MERRA-2 also shows yearly rainfall falling. ERA5 points the same way without reaching significance, and GPM IMERG (1998–2024) shows no trend. So the app calls less rain there "likely", not "confirmed". We also saw the AIRS daytime pass cool and the night-time pass warm in 14 of the 18 places we downloaded. A pattern that repeats across continents points to the instrument, so the app averages the two passes and says why. What both datasets do confirm for Ciudad del Este is warming, of 0.11 to 0.30 °C per decade, and a longer mosquito season. In the 300-city screening, which uses one source, 236 cities show significant warming.

One result, two answers

A trend test is of little use to a family if it stays a chart. So the app gives the same result twice. The first thing a person sees is written in plain words, with one action per sentence. The series, the tests and the sources come after it, under "Learn more: the data for specialists". The plain version adds no data: it rewrites what the other sections already know.

The start screen asks two things: where you live and, optionally, who you are (age, health conditions, work, classes of medicines, housing). It is not a login. There is no account and no server. The answers stay on the device, are saved only after a consent box is ticked, and a button deletes them. An optional line for allergies to medicines is only shown back in the emergency box. Four example profiles let people try the app without answering.

What a person sees

  • 01 My home. One page: this week for you, in short sentences ordered by the profile; the next 3 months; your year in one table of weather events and illnesses by month; whether the climate changed (how many of the eight signals, counting confirmed and likely changes); whether the ground is safe; the chains of consequences; and help and donations (a prototype with fictional examples, plus a link to the directory of Red Cross and Red Crescent societies). The specialist data follow at the end of the page.
  • 02 My health. A heat traffic light with its rule on screen and seven topics ordered by urgency for the place. For medicines that raise risk in the heat, the app explains the risk and says to talk to a doctor. It never tells anyone to stop a medicine.
  • 03 What's ahead. What usually happens here (extreme heat, heavy rain and flooding, tropical storms, tornadoes in the United States, earthquakes, dry spells, frost, landslides, lightning), each with how often, the usual months, why here and the trend since 1981. A health calendar of the address, estimated from temperature and rain, not from case counts. Official guidance before, during and after ten kinds of hazard, safe places within 5 km with walking routes, a kit checklist and a family plan.
  • 04 This week. Seven days with the NOAA heat index, heavy rain, air quality, river discharge, recent earthquakes and open natural events from NASA EONET. For farms: the hours inside the weather limits that Paraguay's Law 3742/2009 sets for spraying.
  • 05 Help and donate. A community board. It is a prototype: reports are stored on the device only, are not verified, and the examples are fictional.
  • Learn more (06 to 09). Two addresses compared side by side. The world panorama of 300 cities, and the 1,500 river mouths that carry the most plastic to the sea in a published model. Thirty-one national health indicators tested with the same trend method, with pressures made by people and the state of nature. Thirty actions with evidence for cities, industry and farms, and 23 real cases, each with its source.

One thing leads to the next. The team's first idea for this project was the cascade: one event leads to the next, and each link is a place to act. On the My home page, each chain that matters at the address appears as a small sum, with the months in which its pieces come together there: heat plus rain is the season of the dengue mosquito; heat and heat illness; heavy rain, then diarrhoea and leptospirosis; cold and respiratory infections; and the chains of dry spells, tropical storms and tornadoes. Opening a chain shows every link, what a family can do, how a community breaks it, and a real case with its source.

See my year. A button walks through the twelve months ahead, one sentence each: the events and illnesses that the records of the place favour in that month, and how likely each is. The month is marked in the year table and the map shows the same month. It describes the usual year of the place. It is not a forecast.

One screen, and a map that follows the reading. On a computer the app opens with the planet where the map is. A click on the planet asks first and then hands the place to the app, and a switch goes between Planet and Map. The map follows the reading: the card being read, a "Show on the map" button, a line of the year table, a health topic, a hazard or a day of the week brings its moving map. When nothing is touched, the map goes through the subjects of the place by itself.

The planet. A globe that starts from space and zooms down to the street, also at https://geocare.life/earth/. It shows the Earth as it was yesterday in true colour (NASA VIIRS), rain (NASA IMERG), wind as moving lines, dust and smoke in the air and ground temperature (NASA MODIS), water in the soil (NASA SMAP), the history of floods, landslides, droughts and cyclones (NASA SEDAC hazard maps), natural events open now (NASA EONET), earthquakes of the last 7 days (USGS) and the app's real cases. A legend says what each layer's colours mean. It also shows the long records: signs of change in 300 cities, storm paths and tornadoes. Tapping any place opens the weather and the air right now; the year of that place in one table of twelve months, estimated from the NASA POWER 1991–2020 climatology of that point and from NOAA storm records, not from case counts; four decades of temperature and rain in one sentence each, worded as a sign from one dataset to be confirmed in the app; and the chains of consequences. A button opens the full app at that place.

Is the ground here safe? A screening in three questions: can the ground slide, can water reach the house, is the soil holding water. It joins the NASA SEDAC Natural Disaster Hotspots maps of landslides, floods and drought, read within about 15 km of the address, with the Copernicus elevation model, heavy-rain days, the river nearby and the NASA POWER trend in topsoil wetness. It is a first look from global data, not a survey of a plot of land.

Maps in motion. The map plays data through time anywhere in the world: rain, ground heat, smoke and dust, vegetation and lightning month by month; the tropical-storm season with every track from 1981 to 2024; the tornado season in the United States; land use from 2001 to 2024; and reported dengue by department of Paraguay from 2019 to 2023. Colours come in discrete classes with their limits in the legend.

Ways in for a first visit. A step-by-step guide for people who are not specialists (https://geocare.life/tutorial/, eight steps with real screenshots). A Demo button that runs seven short demonstrations of the live app with captions, about two minutes in total. Everything is in English, Spanish and Portuguese.

Use of AI. We used an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) to write most of the code and to draft the texts, the translations and the demo slides, under our direction. The idea, the clinical framing and the health priorities are the team's. No language model runs inside the app: every number, verdict and sentence comes from deterministic code. No AI-generated images, audio or video are used. The source files and the repository README carry the same statement.

Benefits and goals

Public plans in our region, such as Brazil's AdaptaSUS and Paraguay's National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change 2022–2030, ask for guidance that reaches each family, risk information at a scale smaller than the city, and a channel for what the community sees. geocare.life is not part of those plans. It is a prototype of those three things. Next steps: review of all health texts by the team's physician, a shared and verified database for community reports, official hazard and evacuation maps where they exist, a Guarani version, and messages for people with little connectivity.

How it works

A static web app with no server of its own: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet, MapLibre GL and Chart.js. All statistics run in the browser with our own implementation of Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen. It works on a phone, is hosted on GitHub Pages, and the code is open under the MIT licence.

Limits we state in the app

  • Gridded climate data describe an area of roughly 25 to 50 km, not a single building.
  • The second dataset (ERA5) comes from a free service with a request limit. It is archived for 24 places and requested live elsewhere. When the limit is reached, verdicts use one source and the app says so.
  • The 300-city panorama and the sentences about temperature and rain on the planet use one source. They are a screening, to be confirmed in the app.
  • The year table, "See my year", the health calendar and the mosquito season describe what the climate of a place usually brings. They are estimates from climate records, not case counts and not a forecast.
  • The ground check is a screening. The NASA SEDAC maps are older global products (floods 1985–2003, drought 1980–2000) on grids of 5 to 50 km. It does not replace an inspection of the land or the advice of civil defence.
  • Health, pesticide, water and sewage figures are national. River plastic values are model estimates.
  • Lightning history is an approximate value read from NASA's LIS climatology (1998–2013). The tornado record covers the United States only. Dengue by department covers Paraguay only.
  • Routes use the street network from OpenStreetMap and are not official evacuation routes. Spraying limits come from Paraguayan law and are a reference elsewhere.
  • The community board is a prototype stored on the device, with fictional examples.
  • Health guidance is general prevention information. It does not replace a medical consultation, and its texts are pending review by the team's physician.
